title: Hollandaise Sauce
subtitle: Classic warm butter and egg yolk emulsion
excerpt: A rich, warm emulsion of egg yolks, reduced white wine vinegar, and clarified butter, seasoned with lemon and cayenne. The sauce for eggs benedict, asparagus, and grilled fish.

recipe.sourceNotes: Hollandaise is one of the five French mother sauces codified by Auguste Escoffier in the early 20th century. Despite the Dutch-sounding name, the sauce is French in origin. It is a warm emulsion, which makes it more technically challenging than cold emulsified sauces such as mayonnaise: the butter is added to warm egg yolks that have been whisked over heat to a ribbon stage, and the whole thing must be kept at a temperature warm enough to maintain the emulsion but not so hot that the eggs scramble. The sauce cannot be reheated successfully once made and should be served immediately. The reduced vinegar base, called a gastrique, gives the sauce its characteristic sharpness.

content.text: The key to hollandaise is temperature control. The yolks must be whisked over simmering water, never boiling: if the water boils and the bowl gets too hot, the eggs will scramble. The butter must be added slowly at first: too much too quickly will break the emulsion. If the sauce looks greasy or separates, remove it from the heat and whisk in a teaspoon of cold water to bring it back. Use the sauce within 30 minutes of making it.

items.preparation: clarified, or gently melted and skimmed

content.text: Put the white wine vinegar, peppercorns, and bay leaf in a small pan. Reduce over medium heat until 1 tablespoon of liquid remains. Strain into a large heatproof bowl, discarding the solids.

Add the egg yolks to the bowl with 1 tablespoon of cold water. Set over a pan of barely simmering water, ensuring the bowl does not touch the water. Whisk continuously for 4 to 5 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and holds a ribbon for 3 seconds when the whisk is lifted.

Remove from the heat. Add the clarified butter drop by drop at first, whisking constantly. Once the sauce begins to thicken and emulsify, add the butter in a slow, steady stream, still whisking. The sauce will be thick and glossy.

Season with lemon juice, cayenne, and salt. The sauce should be sharp enough to cut through the butter. Serve immediately, or keep warm over the pan of hot water with the heat off, whisking occasionally.
